title: One big survey boat or several small ones at equal cost? Fleet sizing for a lawnmower survey
lede: on a line-spacing survey, a fleet of smaller boats bought with the money for one large boat finishes in a median 0.29 to 0.35 of the time and uses a median 0.20 to 0.35 of the energy in the 2,178 to 2,186 of 2,187 cases where it is affordable and wins (never slower); it is affordable only while the payload (sonar) is under half a boat's cost; swath is assumed independent of boat size, which favours the fleet
summary: Milestone 7 of the marine-hull programme. Boats are scaled from the 200 kg, 4 m reference of marine-hull (ITTC 1957 friction line, placeholder wave term); the budget is one boat of 200, 400 or 800 kg and a fleet of mass M/k boats is affordable in number floor(1/cost), cost being a payload share plus a hull share scaling as mass<sup>β</sup>. Over 2,916 cases per speed setting (line length 100 to 1,600 km, payload share 0 to 0.5, β 0.6 to 1, hotel-load exponent 0 to 1, swap 0.5 to 6 h, base 1 to 30 km) the fleet is affordable in 2,187 and finishes sooner in 2,178 to 2,186 of them, never slower (median time ratio among wins 0.35 at best speed, 0.29 at fixed 1 to 1.5 m/s), using a median 0.20 to 0.35 of the energy, because power at a given speed grows with boat mass while swath, set by depth, does not. At a payload cost share of 0.5 no fleet is affordable (arithmetic). Swath independent of size, no sea-state limit, no acoustic or charging constraints, unsourced cost law; these favour the fleet, and a big boat's real case (rougher water, longer-range sonar) is not modelled. Simulation only.
